articles.headline: Police climb a sacred mountain to rescue a tourist
articles.standfirst: A young visitor got trapped on Putucusi, a mountain next to Machu Picchu.
body: A tourist got into trouble on a mountain near Machu Picchu. The mountain is called Putucusi. It is a sacred mountain, and it stands at one end of the Inca city.
The tourist is a 22-year-old man from Ukraine. Last Sunday, a little after noon, he went missing. He became trapped in a place that is very hard to reach. The Ministry of Culture told the police.

Police officers from the Machu Picchu station climbed the steep mountain. They found the man about 100 metres from the start of the climb. The officers helped him and took him safely to the railway line. Then he went to a health centre for a check-up.

More and more visitors want to climb Putucusi because it gives them a new view of Machu Picchu and the Vilcanota River. The top of the mountain is more than 2,560 metres above sea level. The local authorities want to make a route to the top.

going up very quickly, not flat
not in the place where you should be, and nobody knows where you are
the tracks that trains use
a way from one place to another

articles.headline: Formula 1 is coming back to Africa
articles.standfirst: Rwanda will host a Formula 1 race in about 2030, after a new ten-year agreement.
body: Formula 1 is going back to Africa! Rwanda will have a Formula 1 race in about 2030. It will be called the African Grand Prix. The agreement is for ten years.
Formula 1 last raced in Africa in 1993, in South Africa. Since then, the sport has wanted to come back.

The race will be near Kigali, the capital of Rwanda. The new track will be in a town called Bugesera, about 40 kilometres south of the city. The track is not built yet. A new international airport is also being built there.
The track will be fast, with hills and many bends. It will have space for 100,000 people. In the rest of the year, people will also use it for concerts and shows.
A Formula 1 boss said it was a 'landmark moment'. With Rwanda, the sport will race on every continent where people live.

a road made for races

articles.headline: Helicopters and a big plane help to fight forest fires in Cusco
articles.standfirst: Peru's president says two wildfires in the Cusco region are now under control.
body: In the Cusco region, forest fires have been burning in several places. On Tuesday, President Keiko Fujimori said that two of the fires, in the province of Calca, were now under control. She had flown over the area that morning in a helicopter with a general of the Peruvian Air Force. Wildfires can spread quickly, so a fast reaction is very important.

Aircraft are playing an important part in the fight against the fire. Helicopters carry big buckets of water and drop it on the flames. A larger plane, called a C-27J Spartan, is helping as well. It has a tank that holds 1,000 litres of water.

The president also thanked the people who are working on the ground. She said that the forest firefighters and the organised local people are still working hard in Quillabamba. Fighting a fire from the air is useful, but the people on the ground are still very important.

Later, Ms Fujimori planned to hold a working meeting. The air force general, the ministers of Defence and of Agrarian Development and Irrigation, the governor of Cusco, the mayor of Cusco and the firefighters will all be there. Together they will decide where to send the helicopters and the plane next.

glossary.d: a big fire that burns in a forest or on grass and is difficult to stop
a round container with a handle, used to carry water
a large container for liquid
the bright, hot parts of a fire
the person who is the head of a region

articles.headline: The woman whose code helped humans land on the Moon
articles.standfirst: Margaret Hamilton, who led the team that wrote the Apollo 11 software, has died at the age of 90.
body: Margaret Hamilton, one of the great pioneers of computer programming, has died at the age of 90. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced the news on Wednesday. She died on 30 September.

When Hamilton started her career, jobs such as 'software engineer' did not really exist yet. She learned to write programs from a famous weather scientist at MIT. Later, she worked on a system that could find enemy aircraft. Then NASA asked MIT to make the flight software for the Apollo spacecraft, and she was very happy to join the project. She remembered that she was 'the first programmer to join'.

In 1969, only minutes before Apollo 11 was going to land on the Moon, an alarm rang in the spacecraft's computer. The people in charge had to decide whether to stop the mission. They continued, because the software was doing exactly what Hamilton's team had planned. It told everyone about the problem and, at the same time, restarted the most important tasks.
In 2016, President Barack Obama gave her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. In his speech, he said that the astronauts did not have much time, but luckily they had Margaret Hamilton.
Hamilton leaves a daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren.

glossary.d: one of the first people to do or study something new
the programs that tell a computer what to do
an important trip or job with a special aim
a loud sound that warns you about danger
a small round piece of metal given as a prize

What did Hamilton do before she worked on Apollo?
options: She worked on a system that could find enemy aircraft.

options: An alarm rang in the spacecraft's computer.

questions.q: Why did the mission continue?
options: The astronauts did not listen to the alarm.
The software did what the team had planned.

questions.q: What happened in 2016?
options: She won a prize from MIT.
She wrote a book about the Moon.
She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

articles.headline: A child's tomb full of treasures sheds new light on the Moche
articles.standfirst: Archaeologists in northern Peru have found a tomb about 1,400 years old, with 32 ceramic objects and a metal mask.
body: More than 1,400 years ago, the sudden death of a child from the Moche elite led to an important funeral ceremony at the foot of Huaca de la Luna, one of the main temples of this pre-Hispanic society. The temple stands in the Moche valley, near Trujillo, in the La Libertad region of northern Peru.

A few days ago, archaeologists from the Huacas de Moche Project, who were excavating the Uhle funerary platform next to the Courtyard of the Serpents, uncovered the tomb. It may belong to the final period of Moche society. The project director, Carlos Rengifo, told Andina that the discovery is significant because the important tombs found earlier on the platform belonged to adults who had probably reached a certain rank during their lives and were honoured for it after death. A child buried with so many offerings sheds new light on how social status worked.

The tomb measures 1.20 metres long, 70 centimetres wide and 1.20 metres deep, and it has the enclosed structure that is typical of Moche burials. Inside, the team found 32 ceramic objects, including decorated plates and vessels showing bird-shaped figures, prisoners, scenes of sacrifice and combat, and gods. Around the skull there was a kind of metal mask, probably copper and perhaps once decorated, and another piece of metal lay beside the foot bones.

The resident archaeologist, Enrique Zavaleta, said that in more than two decades of excavating at Huaca de la Luna he had never found a tomb with offerings like these. One bottle has attracted particular attention, because bottles of this kind are uncommon in Moche culture. It shows a coastal lagoon, a stretch of water separated from the sea by a strip of sand, with birds.

Rengifo compares Peru's past to an 'enormous puzzle' in which every adobe brick, vessel and fragment helps experts understand what happened and why. He adds that many things we regard as common sense were seen very differently by these ancient societies.

glossary.d: the small group of people with the most power or wealth in a society
connected with a funeral or the burial of a dead person
to dig in the ground to find things from the past
a gift that is given to a god or placed with a dead person
a small piece of something that has broken

questions.q: What makes this discovery different from earlier finds on the Uhle funerary platform?
options: It was the first tomb found on the platform.
The person buried there was a child.
It was built after the Moche period.

questions.q: According to the text, earlier important tombs on the platform belonged to
options: adults who had probably held a certain rank.

questions.q: What did the archaeologists find around the child's skull?
Why does the bottle with the lagoon attract attention?
options: It is the largest vessel in the tomb.
It was found beside the foot bones.
Bottles of this kind are uncommon in Moche culture.

questions.q: What point does Rengifo make with his comparison to a puzzle?
options: Moche history will never be understood.
Every small find helps to explain the past.
Common sense is enough to read the past.

articles.headline: No drones allowed: Beijing bans ownership of the flying machines
articles.standfirst: From 15 November, people in the Chinese capital will not be allowed to keep a drone at home, and owners are rushing to get rid of them.
body: A. Beijing's government announced in September that, from 15 November, it will be forbidden not only to fly drones in the capital but also to own or store one. Before the rules start, owners must take their aircraft out of the city or dispose of them through government-approved buyback and recycling schemes. Anyone who ignores the rules faces confiscation and fines of up to 5,000 yuan.

B. The change has produced long queues at buyback sites, and some owners are being offered less than a quarter of what they paid. Kristine, who lives in Sydney, says her brother bought his drone only a year ago for about 2,000 dollars. He did not want to sell it at a loss, so he posted it to her instead.

C. Others have found a different solution. Matthew Zhang, an aerial photographer, has sent his drone to his parents' home in nearby Tianjin and plans to travel there whenever he needs it. He admits that it is 'definitely inconvenient', but at least he can still use it.

D. Most big Chinese cities already have no-fly zones near airports, military sites and government buildings, but Beijing will be the only one to forbid ownership. Unapproved outdoor flights were banned in August 2025, and the rules became stricter after a small plane crashed into the capital's tallest building in June. The government says the aim is to strengthen the security of the capital.

E. The regulation seems to cover even radio-controlled model aircraft and toy drones, and several online shops, including Taobao, have restricted sales to Beijing addresses. A researcher at a Taiwanese defence institute called the ban 'deeply ironic', because China is the world's biggest maker of consumer drones.

glossary.d: not allowed by a rule or law
to get rid of something
when an official takes something away from you as a punishment
causing difficulty or trouble
an official rule made by a government

articles.instructions: For each question, choose the paragraph (A–E). Each paragraph can be chosen once.

articles.headline: Jonathan the tortoise, 194, may hold clues to a longer life
articles.standfirst: Scientists have analysed the DNA of the world's oldest living land animal and found signs that his cells' tiny 'batteries' have stayed unusually young.
body: Jonathan, a giant tortoise believed to be 194 years old, lives in the grounds of Plantation House, the governor's residence on the South Atlantic island of Saint Helena. As the oldest living land animal, he is a contemporary of Queen Victoria and Charles Darwin, and he has now become an unlikely partner in the age-old human quest to extend lifespan.

An international team led by Benjamin Vaisvil analysed his genetic code. They found a host of variants in most of the biological pathways for ageing that scientists have identified. Together, they help an organism to survive by repairing damaged DNA, regulating its metabolism and fending off cancer. Yet it was something subtler that intrigued the researchers most: chemical patterns on his genes that seem to protect the healthy functioning of his mitochondria, the tiny battery-like structures that power cells. Failing mitochondria have been strongly linked to ageing and to age-related diseases.

The chemical tags involved are known as methyl groups, which typically silence the genes they attach to and change over time. Writing in the journal Science Advances, the team compared the patterns on Jonathan's genes with those of other giant tortoises. On many genes his patterns were similar to those of other old animals, but on genes connected with mitochondrial function they matched those of much younger ones. Stephen Clark, a senior researcher at the Kallel Foundation, said this offers a window on what happens over a very long period, and suggested that Jonathan's mitochondria must be unusually stable.

It is unclear whether, or by how much, this chemical patterning contributes to Jonathan's long life, and Clark said that the team must now test the idea. One possible next step is to ask whether mitochondria can be made young again, or even replaced, to extend longevity.

He arrived on Saint Helena in 1882. When the island's senior veterinary officer, Joe Hollis, took over his care in 2009, he was blind from cataracts, had lost his sense of smell and had a soft, crumbly beak that made it hard to forage. Hollis began feeding him by hand, and within six months to a year Jonathan had regained weight and grown a hard, serrated beak. In April, a fake social-media account spread a false report of his death as part of a cryptocurrency scam, until the governor checked and found him asleep under a tree, 'very much alive'.

articles.headline: China's 'loneliness industry' sells company as well as meals
articles.standfirst: As more people live far from their families, small firms are offering older people practical help and a friendly face.
body: Yang is 91 and lives on the edge of Beijing. Since her husband died, she says, the hardest thing has been the silence: when she wanted to talk to someone, she talked to the television. Glaucoma has left her eyesight failing, so even small tasks, such as adjusting the controls of her air conditioner, had become difficult.

Her situation is far from unusual. Teresa Kuan, an associate professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says that isolation in Chinese cities is made worse by the structure of society and by the way people interact. Rural migrants leave close-knit communities in search of work, and graduates uproot themselves to chase jobs on the other side of the country. In both cases, the support networks they once relied on stay behind.

Out of this gap has grown what is called a 'loneliness industry'. Wang Yingwei, a former mobile-phone salesman, leads a delivery team on electric scooters that brings Yang hot meals twice a day, but their help goes much further. He describes the group as 'community children', trying to put themselves in the shoes of older people. If the tap water is cloudy and full of lime, he installs a filter tank; if a shower is broken, he buys a part and repairs it. Such small things, he argues, can make people much happier. His services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver.

His motive is personal. His father-in-law, who developed Alzheimer's disease, had to move into a nursing home whose conditions Wang considered unacceptable, and he now wants to help older people stay in their own homes for as long as possible. His company currently has four employees, although he says it may grow as demand increases.

Reliable data on the sector is scarce, but operators say it has expanded rapidly in recent years, and the securities company Sinolink valued it at about $7.4 billion in 2025. Zheng Ruizhi, a 75-year-old client whose son lives two hours away, says that since retiring she has had few chances to meet other people; she was recovering from an injury when Wang's team began to visit.

Whether paid company can ever replace the daily presence of family remains an open question. For the moment, though, the customers' answer seems to be a simple one: they would rather have someone at the door than no one at all.
